research_tasks: Before quoting caption-derived lines (SmartLess 2022, Club Random 2025, Happy Sad Confused 2026, Literally! 2026), check them against audio or another transcription; auto-captions garble words (Club Random renders 'trip' as 'chip').

Would people like me?' wording and its continuity with Pratt's turn, but cannot label voices; a human listen at about 38:33 of 'Chris Pratt: Have Mercy!' would close the attribution. Do not use the nearby 'pay attention to what people say about you' / 'being nice is a value and an asset' lines (about 33:55 to 35:04), which could be Lowe's.
Open Anna Faris's May 3, 2021 Unqualified episode audio to read 'we both protected that imagery' in its full context before leaning on it.
The coach anecdote ('I know I'll be famous...') reached Vanity Fair from Entertainment Weekly (2015), which refused automated access. Quote it as VF relaying EW, or open EW manually.

Independent testimony is thin: Gunn, Fuqua and Trevorrow are friendly collaborators, and Faris speaks mostly about herself. If possible, open Rae Dawn Chong's or Mike Schur's own accounts of meeting and casting him (Alan Sepinwall's 2014 Uproxx piece has moved, and the Wayback Machine was offline on 2026-10-29).
Sources disagree on how premature Jack was (seven weeks per the Christian Post, nine per Wikipedia). Say 'premature' without a number unless a primary settles it.

Caption-only material is paraphrased, not quoted, in the draft: SmartLess 2022 (auditioning/salesman joke, 'work to live', farm lake), Happy Sad Confused 2026 (underwear photo and Kevin Feige), Club Random 2025 ('follower of Jesus'). yt-dlp audio download was blocked on 2026-10-29; check these against audio before any of them is upgraded to a direct quote.

sources.title: Cover Story: Chris Pratt's Call to Stardom (Vanity Fair, February 2017 issue)
sources.speaker: Chris Pratt, interviewed at home by Rich Cohen
sources.locator: Sections 'Big Time, Small Town' (wrestling, coach anecdote, father's MS, brother and the army), 'Flair for the Dramatic' (coupon sales, Denver office, Maui, Henry), 'The Outsider' (Rae Dawn Chong, Moneyball, Zero Dark Thirty, Guardians audition). The vanityfair.com text and the archive.vanityfair.com copy both end at the paragraph about his guest spot on Mom; nothing after that point was read.
sources.excerpt: “I’d be devastated,” he said. “Because I put everything into it … “I was like, ‘I don’t know, but I know I’ll be famous and I know I’ll make a shit ton of money.’ ” … a salesman only has one product: himself. “I was great at that,” … I had everyone convinced I’d been off doing this great sales job and making money, and I wasn’t. I had no prospects, no job, was still sort of riding the glory of high school. … ‘I’m more in debt every month. I’m so depressed. I can’t do it.’ … My friends picked me up in a van. They had a cooler of beer. But I was not in a great place. … He said, ‘Jesus told me to talk to you . . .’ At that moment I was like, I think I have to go with this guy. … He says, “Fuck, yeah, I act. Put me in a movie.” … That was the first time I heard someone say, ‘We’re not gonna cast you—you’re too fat.’ So I decided to drop the weight, like in wrestling. … You walk into the room as the character. You let them think the person you are is close to the character they want. You make them think you already are that guy. … He ended up going into the army and told me not to. I think he saw something in me. I was a peculiar kid. … There’s going to be a point in life where you’re going to have to prove that your family is more important to you than show business. … he was a hard man to connect with.
sources.context: Long-form cover profile reported while Pratt cooked at his home during a self-declared work break after Guardians of the Galaxy, Jurassic World and Passengers. The high-school coach exchange is Vanity Fair relaying an Entertainment Weekly interview (the EW original refused automated access and was not opened). The Rae Dawn Chong dialogue is Cohen's reconstruction from Pratt's telling. 'A salesman only has one product: himself' is Cohen's paraphrase of Pratt; 'I was great at that' is Pratt's direct quote. The Jim Carrey line is Carrey's advice as Pratt relayed it.

claims.claim: Retelling the sales venture in 2026, Pratt said he was a great salesman but 'too much of a people pleaser to be a good manager', called it 'definitely a failure', and said that back home, as the former high-school star who 'used to be cool', he felt 'super depressed'.
claims.passage: "I was too much of a people pleaser to be a good manager," he said in 2026.
claims.inference: Consistent across nine years: success at being liked, failure at managing, and a collapse felt as a fall in status. It corroborates the depression in the 2017 account, though not the concealment.
claims.alternative: 'People pleaser' is also the core self-description of a 2 or a 9. Depression after financial failure at 19 is not type-specific.

claims.claim: Pratt says he told his boss he was in debt and depressed and that his mother sent him a ticket home.

claims.inference: The collapse and its emotional cost, in his words.
claims.alternative: Single retelling of a phone call; Not Dead Yet 2026 corroborates the debt and the flight home.

claims.claim: In 2026 Pratt called the sales venture "definitely a failure".
claims.passage: He calls the venture "definitely a failure."
claims.inference: Consistent with the 2017 account.
claims.alternative: Only the shared words of two transcriptions are quoted.

claims.claim: When the sales venture left him in debt and, by his account, depressed, Pratt says he 'had everyone convinced' he was off doing a great sales job and making money, until his mother sent him a ticket home.
claims.passage: I had everyone convinced I'd been off doing this great sales job and making money, and I wasn't. I had no prospects, no job, was still sort of riding the glory of high school.
claims.inference: Facing failure, he kept up a picture of success for people at home rather than report the collapse. Outside acting, this is the clearest instance of protecting how he was seen.
claims.alternative: Ordinary embarrassment in a 19-year-old, or 7-style avoidance of a painful truth. 'Everyone' is hyperbole, and it is a single self-report.

claims.claim: In 2026 Pratt said he had been "kind of like the star of my hometown" and on returning "just felt like super depressed."
claims.passage: He had been "kind of like the star of my hometown," and now "I just felt like super depressed."
claims.inference: Corroborates the 2017 account of a fall in status felt as depression, nine years apart.
claims.alternative: Depression after financial failure at 19 is not type-specific.

claims.claim: Interpretation: what Pratt concealed was the outcome, not the pain.
claims.passage: Pratt talks freely about the depression; what he hid was the result, and he showed success in its place until a friend saw through it and bought him a ticket to Maui.
claims.inference: Labelled in prose as resting on his own retelling, with "everyone" flagged as exaggeration.
claims.alternative: Ordinary embarrassment, or 7-style avoidance of a painful truth.

claims.claim: The Pratts lost their house while he was in high school; in 2026 he linked it to his father's MS ("my dad gets this disease and the bank takes our house away").
claims.passage: His family lost their house while he was in high school, a loss he ties to his father's multiple sclerosis.
claims.inference: Background for his money motivation.
claims.alternative: Diagnosis timing conflicts (senior year per VF, sophomore per Pratt 2026), so no year is named.

claims.passage: I've been money motivated my whole life because we never had anything
claims.inference: Status and scarcity side by side: the star of the school who would not show need. Being admired while hiding lack fits a 3 who earns worth and does not ask for it.
claims.alternative: Childhood poverty explains a money focus in any type, and not asking for things also fits 2 (no needs of one's own) or 9 (not wanting to burden).

claims.inference: Status and hidden need side by side.

claims.claim: In Maui Pratt lived in a van and a tent on the beach and waited tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp.
claims.passage: In Maui, Pratt lived in a van and a tent on the beach and waited tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp.
claims.inference: Biographical; consistent across 2014 and 2017.

claims.claim: Pratt has narrated his Maui year differently across interviews: 'a pretty awesome place to be homeless... a charming time' (2014), 'I was not in a great place' (2017), and 'just having a good time with my friends and enjoying my life' (2022).
claims.passage: "It's a pretty awesome place to be homeless," and called the drinking, weed and short shifts "a charming time."
claims.inference: The same months can be told as idyll or low point depending on the room. That is consistent with an instinct for the version the audience will enjoy.
claims.alternative: Supports the 7 reading: reframing a hard stretch as adventure. Both can be true, partying while lost, and different interviewers asked different questions.

claims.claim: In 2017 Pratt described arriving in Maui: "I was not in a great place."

claims.inference: The darker telling of the same months.
claims.alternative: Partying while lost is compatible with both tellings.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Maui telling shifts with the setting.
claims.passage: Still, the emphasis tracks the room: an adventure for a blockbuster junket, a rescue for a cover story about finding his path.
claims.inference: Prose notes both can be true and the interviewers asked different questions.
claims.alternative: Supports the 7 reading (reframing a hard stretch as adventure).

claims.claim: Pratt says he went with Henry to church and told friends he would change his life.

claims.inference: A turning point initiated by someone else.
claims.alternative: Best read as sincere religious experience rather than type evidence.

claims.passage: "We're not gonna cast you—you're too fat." He told Vanity Fair: "So I decided to drop the weight, like in wrestling." With no money for a trainer, that meant running, crash diets and no alcohol. He got the part.
claims.inference: Sustained self-denial in service of a target image, repeated over years.
claims.alternative: Professional incentive fully explains the dieting itself: action casting demands it of any actor, whatever the type. This claim carries weight only alongside his own framing in c-fun-as-image.

claims.alternative: Action casting demands dieting of any actor.

claims.inference: Another pivotal move initiated by someone else.

claims.inference: Invisibility answered with success rather than confrontation.
claims.alternative: Comic exaggeration in an interview.

claims.passage: Pratt said his brother talked him into posting an underwear photo of the body he had built for _Zero Dark Thirty_, which he thought seemed weird. Later, he said, Marvel's Kevin Feige pulled out that photo and asked whether he could get back in that shape.

type_hypothesis.against: Real counterevidence: he tells the Maui year as 'a pretty awesome place to be homeless... a charming time' (2014). He describes a hyperactive, transgressive childhood (GQ 2015), and Gunn reports a new idea every day; both read 7. He says he wants 'to work to live' and that his mind wanders to fishing his farm's lake (SmartLess 2022). He took a family break on Jim Carrey's advice (VF 2017). He needed his brother to push him to post his transformation photo, which he called 'douchey' (2026). He has kept public faith commitments he says could 'cost me everything' since a 2012 NICU vow (Christian Post 2025). He declines to defend his public image online (Proverbs 26:20). In 2026 he called Hollywood an industry that creates 'idols to burn', said wealth does not fill 'the hole inside of my heart', ranked home above career, and credited his manager, not himself, with being 'calculated and critical' about roles. And many pivotal moves were initiated by others (a friend's Maui ticket, his mother's ticket home, his brother's army advice, an agent's Guardians push), which reads 9. Most of the 3 evidence is self-report in promotional interviews, where any actor talks about image.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: His public persona is the classic 7. He was a hyperactive, disruptive jokester as a child (GQ 2015) and calls the partying Maui year 'a charming time' (2014). There is appetite (food, drink, weed), 'the f words: faith, fishing, fighting', Gunn's 'new idea every day about everything', constant acting-technique experiments, and promises to God that lapsed once each crisis passed (Christian Post 2025). His humor began as a defense against a disapproving father (Men's Health 2022), and 7s use fun to keep pain away. 'To convince people that I was okay' could be a 7 describing his own mask. Andy Dwyer, the role audiences love him for, is an exuberant 7 character.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: When the fun and the image of success pull apart, which does he protect? A 7 protects pleasure and freedom and reframes the loss; a 3 protects how he is seen and pays in pleasure. Pratt's record repeatedly protects the image. After the sales job collapsed he 'had everyone convinced' he was succeeding rather than coming home with a good story (VF 2017). He took the fat-guy persona because it got laughs and 'paying better', then gave it up for years of restriction once 'too fat' cost him Moneyball. He summed up that trade as 'Now I have less fun. I focus more', and called the fun period 'That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay' (GQ 2015). He describes winning rooms by letting them think 'you already are that guy' (VF 2017), and rehearsing 'Would people like me?' (2026). Gunn independently saw him 'juggle to entertain everybody' and not trust himself 'to just be Chris Pratt' (GQ 2015). The 7 reading explains the energy but not why he describes the fun itself as a cast image, or the years-long sacrifice of pleasure. Limit: acting rewards image work, so the non-acting cases carry the most weight (the hidden sales failure; Faris's 'we both protected that imagery'), and each rests on a single source.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Several things the 3 reading does not explain. His faith commitments look like conviction more than image management: a 2018 MTV speech, 2025 statements he expected to cost him with mainstream audiences, and a vow kept since 2012. Yet his framing shifts by audience ('really I'm not a religious person' in 2022). Also unexplained: his discomfort with overt self-promotion (the photo his brother pushed him to post), open crying in interviews, his refusal to fight online narratives, the pattern of other people making his pivotal moves (a 9 signature), and the transgressive childhood humor ('I liked making people feel uncomfortable'). Wing is left open.
